text: The Chinese paddlefish (Psephurus gladius; simplified Chinese: 白鲟; traditional Chinese: 白鱘; pinyin: báixún; literal translation: "white sturgeon"), also known as the Chinese swordfish, is an extinct species of fish that was formerly native to the Yangtze and Yellow River basins in China. It was one of the largest freshwater fish, with records of specimens over 3.6 metres (12 ft) and possibly up to 7 m (23 ft) in length, though definitive evidence of lengths exceeding 3 metres (9.8 ft) is limited, and a reported 7-metre specimen attributed to C. Ping (1931) as cited by John Treadwell Nichols in 1943 is considered likely due to a translation error by Lance Grande and William Bemis in 1991. The last known specimen, a mature female caught in 2003, measured 3.63 metres (11.9 ft) and weighed approximately 200 kilograms (440 lb). A 1996 study estimated the largest females and males could reach 4.363 metres (14.31 ft) and 3.685 metres (12.09 ft), respectively, with FishBase and the World Wide Fund for Nature citing a conservative maximum weight of 300–500 kg (660–1,100 lb). The species was the only member of its genus Psephurus and one of two recent paddlefish (family Polyodontidae), the other being the still-living American paddlefish (Polyodon spathula). Unlike the American paddlefish, which feeds on plankton, the Chinese paddlefish was a piscivorous predator that primarily consumed small to medium-sized fish such as anchovies, cyprinids, gobies, bagrid catfish, and bothid flounders, as well as crustaceans like shrimp and crabs. It had a white underbelly and grey back and head, with dorsal and anal fins located far back on the body, a narrow and pointed paddle-like rostrum between a quarter and a third of total body length, small and round eyes, and a heterocercal tail fin with a well-developed lower lobe. Its skull was more elongate and narrower than that of the American paddlefish and lacked sculpturing, with fewer stellate bones on the rostrum; its teeth were small, sharp, canine-shaped, inward-curling, and fused into the bone in mature adults, with shorter, narrower jaws and a proportionately smaller gape, and the upper jaw not firmly attached to the braincase. The skeleton was largely cartilaginous, and the body lacked scales except for small ones in the caudal peduncle and caudal fin. Juveniles reached about 1 to 1.5 kilograms (2 to 3 lb) and 1 metre (3 ft) by their first winter, and about 3.3 kilograms (7 lb 4 oz) by age one; beyond that, weight gain increased dramatically, reaching about 12.5 kilograms (28 lb) at 1.5 metres (5 ft), with sexual maturity occurring at around 25 kilograms (55 lb). Females were suggested to grow larger than males after maturity, though growth rates were similar prior to that. The species had a lifespan estimated at 29–38 years, though the theoretical maximum was likely higher due to anthropogenic impacts. It was first classified under Polyodon by Eduard von Martens in 1862 and later placed in its own monotypic genus by Albert Günther in 1873; Spatularia angustifolium, named by Johann Jakob Kaup in 1862, is considered a junior synonym. Paddlefish are one of two living families of Acipenseriformes, alongside sturgeons, with the oldest Acipenseriformes records dating to the Early Jurassic (over 190 million years ago), and the oldest paddlefish fossil, Protopsephurus, from the Early Cretaceous in China (around 120 million years ago). The genus Polyodon, containing the American paddlefish, dates back to around 65 million years ago (beginning of the Paleocene), and molecular clock estimates for the divergence between the American and Chinese paddlefish range from 68 to 100 million years ago (middle to Upper Cretaceous). The Chinese paddlefish was native to the Yangtze River basin and its estuary at the East China Sea, historically also found in the Yellow River basin and its estuary at the Yellow Sea, and occasionally in coastal waters of the East and Yellow Seas, including the lower reaches of the Qiantang and Yong rivers in Zhejiang. It primarily inhabited the lower-middle reaches of the Yangtze, which were more prey-rich, and sometimes entered large lakes. Breeding adults migrated from the Yangtze to the lower Jinsha River (upper Yangtze) near Yibin, Sichuan, in fall and winter to spawn in spring (mid-March to early April), with males reaching maturity at 5 years and females at 6 years, and spawning males typically 5–10 years old and females 6–16 years old. Spawning sites were around 500 metres (1,600 ft) long, with a maximum depth of 10 metres (33 ft) and rapid flow, and the bottom was shingly in the lower reaches and muddy/sandy in the upper. Females likely spawned every other year or less frequently. The ovaries contained over 100,000 eggs, each about 2.7 mm (3⁄32 in) across with a sticky surface, which sank and attached to pebbles after fertilization. The species was amphidromous, with juveniles migrating 2,750 kilometres (1,710 mi) downriver after hatching in the upper Yangtze, reaching the Yangtze estuary near Shanghai by 4–5 months of age, then spending time in brackish and saline coastal waters, before migrating back upriver as subadults at 1.5–2 years old and progressing up to spawning grounds between Chongqing and Yibin. It was largely solitary and occupied the lower-mid water column, and was noted for being a strong swimmer. It used passive electroreception via ampullae in the head and rostrum to detect prey. The species was first named as Polyodon by von Martens in 1862, and later moved to Psephurus by Günther in 1873. The last records in the Yellow River basin and its estuary date to the 1960s, with declines noted between the 13th and 19th centuries, and annual harvests reaching 25 tonnes by the 1970s. A 2024 study estimated the spawning-age population in 1980 to be around 3,000. In 1983, the Chinese government banned fishing of the species due to its decline. Small numbers were still caught in the 1980s (e.g., 32 in 1985), and young individuals were seen as late as 1995. Attempts to establish a captive breeding program failed due to the rarity of the fish and difficulty in keeping adults alive. Since 2000, only two confirmed live sightings have occurred in the Yangtze basin: a 3.3-metre (10 ft 10 in), 117-kilogram (258 lb) female caught in Nanjing in 2002, which died despite rescue efforts, and a 3.52-metre (11 ft 7 in), 160-kilogram (350 lb) female accidentally caught in Yibin in January 2003 by fisherman Liu Longhua, which was radio-tagged and released but the tag failed after 12 hours. From 2006 to 2008, a research team from the Chinese Academy of Fisheries Science in Jingzhou failed to catch any paddlefish, though two possible specimens were detected via hydroacoustic signals. A 2019 study by scientists from the Yangtze River Fisheries Research Institute concluded the species was extinct based on its absence from extensive capture surveys between 2017 and 2018, estimating extinction between 2005 and 2010, with functional extinction occurring by 1993. The IUCN Species Survival Commission Sturgeon Specialist Group unanimously agreed to declare it extinct on 15 September 2019, and the official IUCN Red List status was formally updated to "extinct" in July 2022. The primary cause of extinction was the construction of the Gezhouba Dam in 1981, which blocked migration to upriver spawning grounds and fragmented the population, effectively preventing reproduction and leading to long-term population collapse. Overfishing also contributed significantly, as the species was heavily overfished at all life stages, from fry to adults, compounded by its long generation time. The fish was fished for caviar, though it made up less than 1% of total Yangtze fish catches by weight in the late 20th century. Historical references include a gold belt from the Jinsha site (c. 1000 BC) with paddlefish depictions, mentions in the Classic of Poetry (11th–7th century BC) as a sacrificial animal, the Huainanzi (2nd century BC) stating it was attracted to music, Guo Pu’s Jiang Fu (Eastern Jin), and a 9th-century Tang dynasty text suggesting killing the fish could cause rain. It appears in numerous historical Chinese paintings, and Sichuanese fishermen referred to its large size, with common names comparing its rostrum to an elephant’s trunk.
